sentences.text: Last time, Alder's ratio came out at 1.62, and Dune's at 1.46. So Alder looks the worse of the two.
But put their curves side by side. Dune's is the higher one, at every level of risk.
Whoever you are, your chance of readmission is greater at Dune.
So how did Alder end up with the bigger ratio?
The answer is in who each clinic treats. And it leads to a second way of measuring.
Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: swap the patients.
Start with lower-risk patients. At the reference, their chance is 18%. At Alder it is 34%, and at Dune, 36.
At either clinic, that is close to double.
Now the higher-risk patients: 62% at the reference, 80 at Alder, 81 at Dune.
A much smaller multiple, about 1.3. It is Episode 5 again: the same gap in odds means less, in proportion, when the risk is already high.
Here is the catch. Of Alder's 30 patients, 24 are lower-risk, where the multiple is near 2. Dune's 12 are split evenly.
So Alder's ratio is the larger because of who Alder treats, not because its curve is higher.
Give Dune Alder's patients, and Dune's ratio would be 1.68.
Last time's ratio judges each clinic on its own patients. It does not line clinics up against one another.
So turn last time's method around. Keep each clinic's curve, and swap the patients.
Give every clinic the same crowd: all 103 patients in the cast. 57 lower-risk, 46 higher-risk.
Under Alder's curve, that is 57 patients at 34%, and 46 at 80%. Add up the chances: 56.2 readmissions.
56.2 out of 103. If everyone had gone to Alder, the model expects 54.5% to be readmitted.
That is Alder's direct rate. One clinic's curve, everyone's patients.
Now every clinic. Alder, 54.5%. Birch, 32.2. Cedar, 37.6. Dune, 55.9.
And Dune is back above Alder. On the same patients, the higher curve always gives the higher rate.
Elm's figure, 0.7%, is hatched. It rests on a gamma that only records where the fitting stopped.
One trap. The overall rate was 41%, but that is not the yardstick here. Cedar, the reference clinic itself, comes out at 37.6.
Everyone at the reference would have 38.8 readmissions, the same 38.8 we met last time. So compare a direct rate with the reference clinic's, not with the overall rate.
Against Cedar's 37.6, Alder's 54.5 is 1.45 times as high. Last time's ratio said 1.62.
Both are right. They answer different questions.
Last time's question: how did this clinic do with the patients it actually treated? That is the one to ask when a clinic is held to account.
Today's question: how would this clinic do with everyone's patients? That is closer to what someone choosing between clinics wants to know.
And neither is a rate that anyone actually experienced.
A common footing has a price. Alder treated only 6 higher-risk patients. Its direct rate asks its curve about 46.
Two-thirds of that 56.2 comes from patients of a kind Alder hardly saw.
For Elm it is starker. Elm treated no higher-risk patients at all. Its figure rests entirely on the model's assumption that every clinic's curve has the same shape.
In the crowd of 200, the two measures agree closely. Yet between the two rankings, four providers move ten places or more.
A ranking can shift with the question, before luck has even entered.
Let's gather it up.
Last time: a clinic's own patients, on the reference curve.
This time: everyone's patients, on the clinic's own curve.
The second compares like with like, but asks each clinic about patients it never treated. Always say which one you are reporting.
One question is still open. Alder had 13 readmissions where the reference expects 8. A real difference, or luck?
Next time: unequal coins.
This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
